item.content:encoded:
Several years ago, while living in Bayview Heights, one of my neighbours was burgled. Police arrived with a sniffer dog, which picked up the scent and tracked it down the road to a nearby squatter settlement. When officers entered the settlement and questioned residents, nobody was willing to identify the suspects. Whether it was fear, loyalty or simply a refusal to cooperate, the investigation reached a dead end. After speaking with police officers that day, and on subsequent occasions, I came to understand that this was not an isolated incident. It appeared to be a commonly occurring theme.

ACROSS the Suva-Nausori corridor, police are regularly called to investigate crimes that eventually lead them into squatter settlements. Law enforcement officers also conduct frequent drug operations in squatter settlements as Fiji grapples with an escalating drug crisis.

Now, I am in no way saying that every single person living in a squatter settlement is involved in drugs and crime.

But many squatter settlements have become environments where drugs and crime flourish, where criminals can hide more easily, and where police operations become more difficult.

Fiji’s squatter settlement problem has grown rapidly over the past two decades.

Government reports estimate that around one quarter of Fiji’s urban population now lives in more than 200 squatter settlements, most of them concentrated around the Suva-Nausori corridor and other urban centres.

We should be honest about what squatting is. It is, by definition, the unlawful occupation of land. Compassion for those facing hardship does not change that legal reality.

This crisis did not emerge overnight. It is, in large part, a legacy of the former FijiFirst Government, whose failure to confront the growth of illegal settlements allowed the problem to deepen.

Today, there are renewed calls to provide electricity, water and other services to settlements that remain unlawful. One has to ask: have political votes become more important than tackling the growing problems of drugs, crime and the increasing strain on Fiji’s infrastructure?

There is also an issue of fairness that is rarely discussed. Families who obey the law must pay rent or mortgages, rates, utilities and the many costs of living in Fiji’s urban centres. Those occupying land illegally avoid many of these costs, effectively allowing them to live beyond their means while enjoying the same access to jobs and services.

Worse still, this privilege is sometimes exploited. In 2019, a newspaper investigation revealed that some occupants of squatter settlements were renting out rooms, extending their homes to accommodate paying tenants and even selling structures built on land they did not legally own.

There is also the issue of urban capacity. Every new squatter settlement places additional pressure on roads, water supply, electricity networks, waste management, schools and healthcare services. Infrastructure designed for one population must suddenly serve many more people, often without the corresponding investment needed to support that growth. The result is declining service quality that affects everyone.

Crime is another consequence that cannot be ignored. Fiji Police statistics show theft, burglary and drug offences have all increased in recent years, while national drug cases have risen sharply, driven particularly by methamphetamine and marijuana.

Squatter settlements have become a convenient cover for criminal activity, allowing offenders to hide among densely populated communities and making police investigations more difficult. Academic research in Fiji has also identified some settlements as developing reputations as crime “hotspots.”

Perhaps the greatest cost is to the rule of law itself. When governments tolerate the illegal occupation of land for years on end, they send the message that some laws can simply be ignored if enough time passes or enough political pressure is applied.

Brazil’s favelas provide one example that should have Fijians very worried.

Many began as small squatter communities built by people with nowhere else to live.

Over time, they evolved into densely populated neighbourhoods where organised crime and drug trafficking gained influence, making effective policing increasingly difficult.

Fiji is heading down this road. While we are not yet facing the scale of Brazil’s favelas, the warning signs are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. If the growth of illegal settlements continues unchecked, accompanied by rising drug activity, crime and mounting pressure on public infrastructure, the challenge will only become more difficult and more expensive to solve.

Ignoring illegal settlements will not make them disappear. Romanticising them will not solve the problems they create.

This is a real and growing problem that Fiji can no longer afford to ignore.

We need leaders with the courage to make difficult decisions in the national interest, not politicians willing to sacrifice the country’s future for a few thousand votes. If we fail to act now, the price paid by future generations will be far greater than the political cost of acting today.

item.title: HEALTH I Sikiti, 93, and her life secrets
item.description: Sikiti Kaisuva is a rare gem. At 93 years old, she still reads without the aid of spectacles and speaks with remarkable clarity, warmth and vigour. Her sharp mind and infectious spirit are as striking today as they have been throughout a life rich in experience and wisdom.
item.content:encoded:
Sikiti Kaisuva is a rare gem. At 93 years old, she still reads without the aid of spectacles and speaks with remarkable clarity, warmth and vigour.

Her sharp mind and infectious spirit are as striking today as they have been throughout a life rich in experience and wisdom.

Welcoming The Sunday Times team into her home near Korovou Town in Tailevu, Mrs Kaisuva reflected on the simple yet enduring pillars she believes have blessed her with a long and fulfilling life—faith, wholesome food and a loving family.

A proud mother of nine children and grandmother to 36 grandchildren, she says her greatest blessing has been raising a family grounded in peace, happiness and love.

Those virtues, nurtured over generations, remain the foundation of her close-knit family whose bond continues to grow stronger with time.

“I owe my long life to God and God alone,” she said unabashedly, a Bible by her side, tattered by many years of overuse.

“For someone my age, I spend most of my time meditating…I read the Bible and pray as if they are food and water. There’s nothing else to do, I just wake up, sing, worship and just give thanks for the good life I enjoy.”

Sikiti hails from Nukunuku, Lakeba in Lau and was raised by dedicated Christian parents whose tutelage laid a firm spiritual foundation for her and her siblings, encouraging them to live with purpose and compassion.

Having witnessed nearly a century of change, Sikiti has seen generations come and go, along with the rise of diseases and the growing number of lives cut short far too soon.

While the trend does not surprise her, it deeply concerns her. She believes many of today’s health challenges stem from changing lifestyles, poor eating habits and a departure from the simple, disciplined way of life that sustained her generation.

Government statistics show that diabetes prevalence in Fiji has climbed to between 16.5 and 17 per cent, up from 14.6 per cent in 2011.

Furthermore, 98.5 per cent of adults aged 18 to 69 have at least one risk factor for NCDs, while almost half live with three or more.

More than 68 per cent of adults are overweight or obese, with obesity affecting 40 per cent of the population, the majority of them women.

Hypertension affects 36.6 per cent of Fijians, yet almost half of those living with the condition do not know they have it.

Diabetes Fiji executive officer Kini Marawa this week said these figures should be treated as a wake-up call for government, businesses, civil society, sporting organisations and faith-based groups.

He said the issue could not be left to the health sector alone. It is about roping in government bodies, corporate entities, civil society organizations, sports federations, and faith-based institutions to work on a united front against NCDs.

For Sikiti, good health is neither accidental nor complicated.

It is the result of deliberate choices made every day, guided by faith, nourished by nature and rooted in principles she has followed throughout her life.

She believes the answers to living well have always existed, if only people are willing to return to them.

“I cannot speak for others but how I’ve lived my life tells me that we should treat our bodies like a sacred temple and only feed and quench it with super foods, and I mean garden produce like fresh fruits and vegetables,” Sikiti said.

“My Bible tells me what to eat and what not to eat. So you can’t expect good health if you are eating foods you are supposed to stay away from. Eat and drink only the best.”

Being an Adventist Christian, Sikiti loves her green vegetables and fruits and makes sure she has a healthy supply.

She sources her meat protein largely from fish and other white meats and stays away from red meats.

“I have never smoked and I have never tasted yaqona or alcohol.

There’s another secret to Sikiti’s long life. She inherited genes for longevity.

She says she has an older brother, Jale, who is 102-years and a younger brother, Tuiloma who is 91. Her only sister, Selai, who visited her on her birthday last weekend is around 87 years old.

One can only imagine the joy and laughter that fill the air whenever the siblings reunite to celebrate a special family occasion.

That moment came two years ago when Jale celebrated his 100th birthday—a milestone that brought generations of the family together to honour a life well lived, rekindle cherished memories and create new ones.

Sikiti feels the combination of faith, food and family are the real reasons behind her long life.

Taking away one, she believes, would upset the balance that has sustained her for more than nine decades, because each has played an equally important role in shaping the healthy, fulfilling life she has enjoyed.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I A mission into the mountains
item.description: MORE than 150 years after Reverend Thomas Baker’s death, two accounts continue to shape the story of the missionary’s final journey into the mountains of Viti Levu. One survives through the oral traditions of Navatusila, carefully preserved by generations of chiefly descendants. The other was recorded by Baker’s close friend, Methodist minister John S. Austin.
item.content:encoded:
MORE than 150 years after Reverend Thomas Baker’s death, two accounts continue to shape the story of the missionary’s final journey into the mountains of Viti Levu.

One survives through the oral traditions of Navatusila, carefully preserved by generations of chiefly descendants. The other was recorded by Baker’s close friend, Methodist minister John S. Austin.

Together, they offer contrasting perspectives on one of Fiji’s most enduring historical events.

Some lives are remembered not simply for the way they ended, but for the convictions that carried them to their final moments.

For Reverend Baker, the rugged mountains of Viti Levu were more than an isolated frontier. They were home to communities he believed had yet to hear the Christian message. Despite the dangers that lay beyond the established coastal mission stations, he willingly accepted the challenge of serving in Fiji’s remote interior.

More than a century and a half after his death in 1867, Baker’s final journey continues to be retold through different narratives. While both recount the same tragic outcome, they differ in the events that led to his death, illustrating how history can be preserved through both written records and oral tradition.

One account was written by Baker’s longtime friend, Methodist minister John S. Austin, who knew him before he left Australia for Fiji. The other emerged generations later through stories carefully preserved by the descendants of the Navatusila chief associated with the incident. Although both recount Baker’s final expedition into Fiji’s mountainous interior, the oral tradition offers a perspective handed down within the community where the events unfolded.

Before Thomas Baker became one of Fiji’s best-known missionaries, those who knew him remembered him as a man deeply committed to his faith.

Among them was John.S. Austin, who reflected on their friendship in his autobiography Missionary Enterprise and Home Service. The two men had worked together in the Chippendale Circuit in Australia before Baker answered what Austin described as “the call of God to the Mission Field” and departed for Fiji.

Austin never forgot the moment news reached Australia that his friend had been killed.

“It was toward the end of the year 1867 that we received the news of the massacre of the Reverend Thomas Baker and his companions in the interior of one of the Islands of Fiji,” he wrote.

For Austin, the loss was deeply personal.

After arriving in Fiji, Baker spent several years working among coastal communities before accepting what Austin described as one of the mission’s most challenging appointments.

In 1865, he was stationed in the interior of Viti Levu, where Christianity had yet to gain a foothold.

Austin described the region as being “right on the border of what was still cannibal Fiji,” reflecting both the language and perceptions of nineteenth-century missionaries.

Although separated by hundreds of kilometres, the two friends remained in contact through letters carried by passing ships. Those exchanges, Austin recalled, revealed Baker’s unwavering commitment to his work despite the hardships of serving in such a remote region.

Austin remembered Baker as a man who rarely chose the easier road.

Instead, he continued travelling into isolated mountain villages where Christianity had not yet reached. Austin described these expeditions as “raids on the heathen portion of his large circuit”.

By July 1867, Baker believed the time had come to venture even farther into Fiji’s mountainous interior.

He assembled a mission party comprising a native minister, two teachers and seven students. Their purpose was to carry the Christian message into distant communities beyond the established mission stations.

According to Austin, Christian chiefs warned Baker of the dangers ahead and urged him not to continue. Yet Austin believed his friend accepted those risks out of conviction rather than recklessness.

“He had a passion for the souls of the heathen, and this was shared by his brave comrades,” Austin wrote.

He said the group departed fully aware of the dangers before them.

“And so, they started, willing to die, if need be, for the sake of Him who died for them.”

Both accounts agree that signs of danger emerged before the missionaries reached their destination.

Austin wrote that while travelling through the interior, Baker stayed in a village where a chief held a grudge against him. Rather than confronting the missionary directly, the chief allegedly sent a messenger carrying a whale’s tooth to another chief farther along the route, asking that Baker be killed.

The oral history recorded more than a century later also refers to a whale’s tooth being sent ahead following a disagreement earlier in the journey. Although the two narratives differ in many respects, this is one detail on which they broadly agree.

According to Austin, Baker and his companions arrived at another village on a Saturday afternoon. Hoping to remain for the Sabbath before continuing their work, they instead sensed hostility among their hosts.

Concerned, Baker asked the chief to provide a guide so the party could leave immediately.

Instead, the chief insisted they stay overnight, assuring them a guide would be provided the following morning.

item.title: OUR FASCINATING WORLD I Surface, upper air wind measuring

item.content:encoded:
There is an old saying across the Pacific that everybody is a weatherman. You step out of your bure early morning, glance at the angle of the coconut fronds, look at the clouds in the sky, then also feel the humidity clinging to your skin, and instinctively know whether to grab an umbrella or prepare for a hot day.

Yet, behind every official weather bulletin, tropical cyclone warning, and agricultural advisory lies a quiet, precise army of instruments. Day and night, rain or shine, these mechanical and electronic sentinels stand watch across our islands and seas, translating the invisible moods of the atmosphere into hard numbers.

Over the coming weeks, this series will explore the complete toolkit of the weather, climate and atmospheric sciences. Across ten dedicated parts, we will examine wind instruments, rainfall, temperature and humidity, atmospheric pressure, upper-air observations, severe weather tracking, evaporation and soil moisture, solar radiation, sunshine, weather map plotting, analysis and weather forecasting, and weather variability and change issues.

Wind is air in motion driven by pressure gradients, but measuring this invisible river requires clever physics. At the surface, wind vanes use aerodynamic drag to align with the flow, while cup anemometers measure speed as moving air creates differential pressure across hemispherical cups, spinning an internal generator.

During a tropical cyclone, wind behavior turns chaotic. Meteorologists distinguish between sustained averages and violent, sudden gusts caused by turbulence and downdraughts. To capture these extremes—and the fierce vertical wind profiles stretching into the upper air—forecasters rely on ruggedized surface sensors and radar-tracked pilot balloons, ensuring we understand the full mechanical fury of the storm before it makes landfall.

Long before automated weather stations dotted our archipelagos, human survival relied entirely on reading the wind. Ancient Polynesian voyagers and early global navigators mastered the subtle shifts of the trade winds, ocean swells, and cloud structures to cross vast oceanic expanses. In the marine environment, wind is the primary driver of surface currents and wave generation.

Before mechanical anemometers were common, observers relied on empirical descriptive tools like the Beaufort scale, established by Admiral Sir Francis Beaufort in 1805. The scale originally graded winds from Force 0 (calm) to Force 12 (hurricane) based entirely on how a full-rigged Royal Navy ship reacted to the canvas.

At its core, the mechanical cup anemometer is a masterpiece of simple aerodynamic design. Typically consisting of three or four hemispherical cups mounted symmetrically on horizontal arms, it exploits the drag differential between the hollow concave face and the smooth convex back of the cups. When wind blows, the force exerted on the concave side is significantly greater than on the convex side, producing a net torque that rotates the central axis.

Modern calibration ensures that the rotational velocity is directly proportional to the true wind speed. For directional measurements, the companion wind vane utilizes a vertical fin design where aerodynamic pressure forces the tail downwind, aligning a potentiometer or digital encoder to yield precise directional degrees. Together, these surface tools provide the continuous baseline data essential for local forecasting and engineering design.

Surface measurements tell us only what is happening at ground level, but the atmosphere is a three-dimensional thermodynamic engine. To understand how weather systems develop, meteorologists must track winds aloft. This practice historically began with pilot balloons, or “pibals”—small, highly visible hydrogen- or helium-filled balloons released into the atmosphere.

As the balloon ascends at a predetermined, constant rate of ascent, observers track its precise trajectory using a specialized optical theodolite. By noting the azimuth and elevation angles at regular minute intervals, forecasters can apply trigonometry to compute wind speed and direction at successive altitude layers, revealing the steering currents that guide weather systems across the globe.

While visual tracking with an optical theodolite works well under clear skies, tropical skies are frequently choked with clouds, rain, and turbulence. To pierce through overcast conditions, meteorologists transitioned to radio-windfinding and radar tracking of upper-air targets.

Specialized radar reflective targets or small transponders attached to ascending balloons allow tracking equipment on the ground to monitor the balloon’s precise coordinates regardless of visibility. By continuously recording these spatial shifts over time, upper-air radar tracking calculates high-resolution wind profiles through the boundary layer and middle troposphere, supplying vital data streams for aviation safety and severe weather prediction.

The ultimate evolution of vertical sounding is the radiosonde—a battery-powered telemetry instrument package suspended beneath a weather balloon. As the balloon ascends through the troposphere and stratosphere, the radiosonde continuously measures ambient temperature, relative humidity, and barometric pressure, while its position is tracked via advanced navigation systems like GPS to derive exact upper-wind vectors.

Crucially, these wind measurements are mapped directly to standard isobaric pressure levels (such as the 850, 500, and 200 hPa surfaces). This alignment allows forecasters to visualize upper-level troughs, ridges, and jet streams on synoptic charts, providing the foundational 3D framework required for modern numerical weather prediction.

Wind data is not just for weather forecasting; it dictates the safety and economics of global aviation. Take-off and landing performance depend heavily on headwinds, which increase aerodynamic lift over the wings at lower ground speeds, shortening the required runway roll. Conversely, tailwinds require longer runways and stricter weight limits.

Near the surface, low-level wind shear—an abrupt, violent shift in wind speed or direction over a very short distance—presents a lethal hazard during final approach, threatening to instantly strip away aircraft lift. Ground-based anemometers and Doppler radar systems monitor these invisible traps, while airlines rely on accurate upper-wind forecasts to optimize flight paths, saving millions in jet fuel and keeping Pacific skies secure.

Every isolated measurement collected by a cup anemometer, pilot balloon, or radiosonde serves as a vital data point in a global network. When transmitted via international telecommunication systems, these observations are assimilated into massive numerical weather prediction models run by meteorological centres worldwide.

These models process surface friction, Coriolis forces driven by Earth’s rotation, and pressure gradient inputs to simulate how global wind belts—such as the Hadley cells and mid-latitude westerlies—evolve over time. What begins as a local breeze rustling a backyard weather station ultimately contributes to the planetary-scale equations that forecast tomorrow’s weather and next season’s climate anomalies.

Beyond day-to-day forecasting, continuous and consistent wind measurement is an indispensable pillar of climate science. Long-term observational archives allow climatologists to detect subtle shifts in regional wind patterns, monsoon intensities, and tropical cyclone climatology over decades.

As global temperatures rise and atmospheric circulation cells shift, tracking changes in surface wind speeds and upper-air jet stream behaviour helps scientists model future environmental impacts on sea levels, ocean mixing, and island ecosystems. Through meticulous instrumentation from the surface to the stratosphere, we ensure that the invisible story of the wind continues to guide our resilience in a changing world.

item.title: WORLD MANGROVE DAY I The crabs are coming back

item.content:encoded:
SULIASI Nasau remembers when the mangroves held everything together. Not just the coastline, but the kitchen, the medicine cabinet, the wedding ceremony, the roof above one’s head.

Suliasi Nasau is the turaganikoro of Naiseralagi, one of the five partner villages for the Kiwa RESTORE Project in Navitilevu Bay in Ra Province. He has watched the mangrove forests thin over the decades, and he has watched them begin to come back.

The mangrove uses, he lists, are layered and specific. Mangrove wood built the posts of the traditional bures, because it lasted. Dry, it could hold a structure for eight to ten years. The bark produced dark dye pressed into tapa worn by chiefs. The stems were cut and scraped and woven into salusalu, the garlands placed around the necks of guests at ceremonies. And the roots of certain species were used as medicine, specifically as a cough treatment for children.

“Mangroves are used in firewood, housing, clothing and even herbal medicine,” Nasau says. “It has a lot of uses in our traditional lives in the village.”

The forest was also where families fished, where women set their traps and men anchored their canoes.

In the olden days, Nasau says, people knew which trees to cut.

‘They took the mature ones and left the young trees to grow,” he said.

They called it selective cutting. It was not written down anywhere. It was simply understood.

“Traditional knowledge is science, but just given different names,” he says. “Message remains the same when it comes to restoration of mangroves.”

That knowledge did not disappear entirely, but it frayed. Nasau traces the loss of mangroves to several causes. Cyclones and floods stripped away the mangrove forests that had taken decades to establish. Shipping vessels introduced oil spills that killed whole sections of the forest. And then there was the cutting.

In the towns, bundles of mangrove wood sell at roadside stations for four dollars. Six sticks in a bundle. The men doing the cutting are mostly young, and they take the green wood because it is easier to cut than the dry, Nasau says.

“They spoiling them for money,” Nasau says.

He knows what it costs. When the mangrove forest shrinks, so does everything it supports. Crabs, fish, coastal protection, ceremony. The connection between the forest and daily life is direct and measurable, and the people of Navitilevu Bay have measured it the hard way.

Severe Tropical Cyclone Winston changed everything when it made landfall in February 2016. Ra Province was among the hardest hit.

Before the storm, women from Naiseralagi could fill a fifty-kilogram bag with catch in three to four hours. After Winston, eight to nine hours yielded less than ten kilograms. The fish and crabs had gone. So had the seafood on the table.

“Now we depend more on rourou, bele and food we can make from flour,” Naiseralagi Women’s Group Treasurer Siteri Vuru says.

She added fried food bought from town had replaced the seafood.

“For healthier life, we need the mangroves,” Analaisa Dobui, the secretary of the women’s group added.

Analaisa said they shifted where they fished.

They had to go deeper, further out. It was more work and less return.

The restoration work in Navitilevu Bay began under the DFAT’s Fiji Blue Carbon Project and has continued under the Kiwa RESTORE Project, supported by the Kiwa Initiative and implemented by Conservation International. Five villages are involved: Naiseralagi, Barotu, Nanukuloa, Navuniivi, and Matawailevu.

To date, 15.47 of the targeted 20 hectares of mangrove have been restored across the bay. Community members carry out potting exercises and planting. The work is done in partnership with the iTaukei communities – the same people who have always depended on these mangroves.

The signs of recovery are coming in from the water.

“Mud crabs are coming back, they are getting bigger,” Nasau says. “With the restoration now, people are getting good size crab.”

The women say the same. Crabs are returning. Fish are appearing closer to the shore again. They do not have to go as far out as they did in the years after Winston.

There are rules now about size. Small crabs go back into the water. Only the large ones are taken. The community holds that line.

At the village meetings, Nasau reminds people to leave the young growth alone.

He says it the same way his forefathers would have said it, because the instruction has not changed.

“We tell people in the village during the village meeting since we are doing the restoration, please refrain from cutting green mangroves.”

Few people in Naiseralagi can still build a traditional bure. But in some villages, chiefs still sit inside chiefly houses held up by mangrove posts, their walls hung with tapa cloth dyed with mangrove bark, their guests wearing salusalu woven from scraped mangrove stems.

item.title: REFLECTION I Beyond the clouds – Kite carries message of hope and peace
item.description: This poem was inspired by the childhood charm of days past. Once upon a time, children held hands and danced around a tree to celebrate the commencement of a new season.
item.content:encoded:
This poem was inspired by the childhood charm of days past.

Once upon a time, children held hands and danced around a tree to celebrate the commencement of a new season.

Children crafted chains and crowns from a carpet of dainty daisy flowers that adorned the grass (my own childhood).

When a toy for a child was an Abacus or a minature sail boat crafted of wood by their grand-father.

When the bonds of friendship were formed from a message in a bottle.

When exercise for a child was a skipping rope or climbing a tree or rides in a wheelbarrow around the farmyard.

Sometimes, it was a tyre swing attached securely to a tree branch or a swim in the stream.

There was another beloved play item for children – the kite.

The sky would be serenaded in a sea of shades brilliant, as children learnt the art and craft of kite making at home.

Kites would fly high on a mid-morning Sunday sky until the sun set to rest. Soft and durable fabrics were utilised in the creation of kites so the winds could carry them far and nigh.

The kite was a childhood charm that hopefully, will one day serenade the skies again.

The present status of many lands in discord and distress and spirits in silent strife and stress was another point of inspiration for this poem.

The kite as a symbol is often depicted as a representation of freedom, a joyous spirit, childhood innocence and nature. It is free to float blissfully beyond the clouds, just as many knees bend in prayer for the serenity and salvation of their sufferings, their lands, their people, their neighbours and their earth.

The kite that glides across the sky, receiving her strength from the positive energy of nature:

The sunshine that radiates the beauty of her creation.

The raindrops that reveal her resilience to fly high.

The clouds that bow to the aura of her presence as she adorns the sky in her serene silence.

The regal shades of sunset that light the path of her journey.

The cord that binds her to earth so she may return to the sanctuary of her home when her day is done.

The gaze of the kite sees all in her path and if she could relate the sights she beholds, there would be tales of peace and prosperity; of love and whispers of war; of harmony and words of harm; of hopeful hearts and weary spirits; of construction and implications of destruction…..

The kite is a symbol of simplicity, serenity, childhood charm, peace and a well of providence, from whence the people seek refuge in the comfort of her presence. May her presence in the sky above warm hearts and weaken hands that seek to inflict harm.

The chapter of childhood was a sacred sanctuary for many people who today, only see the winds of conflict and challenge. Some adjust to the winds; some stall in a windstorm and some sail through the winds because their gaze is affixed to the light beyond the winds – just like a kite.

Such are the choices that people can seek recourse to when the winds blow in a direction not compatible with their life journey. It is not always the easiest solution but eventually, all winds subside to a gentle breeze – and like a kite, we sail forward.

The kite as a symbol is often depicted as a representation of freedom, a joyous spirit, childhood innocence and nature. Picture: WWW.PEXELS.COM/Ty Nguyen

item.title: FOCUS I Beyond the algorithm – lessons from Pope Leo
item.description: As governments, technology companies and policymakers race to harness the promise of artificial intelligence (AI), the conversation is often dominated by questions of speed, efficiency and economic opportunity and the Pacific is no exception. This week, Fiji hosted the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 at Denarau, where regional leaders, telecommunications experts and industry representatives gathered
item.content:encoded:
As governments, technology companies and policymakers race to harness the promise of artificial intelligence (AI), the conversation is often dominated by questions of speed, efficiency and economic opportunity and the Pacific is no exception.

This week, Fiji hosted the Pacific Fiber Conference 2026 at Denarau, where regional leaders, telecommunications experts and industry representatives gathered to discuss AI infrastructure, subsea connectivity and the digital future of the Pacific.

The conference reflected the undeniable reality that AI is no longer a distant concept but an emerging force that will increasingly shape Pacific societies.

Yet, amid discussions about fibre networks, computing power and innovation, another voice has entered the global AI debate which shifts attention away from machines and back towards people.

In his first social encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (“The Greatness of Humanity”), released in May this year, His Holiness Pope Leo XIV argued that artificial intelligence is ultimately not a technological challenge, but a human one.

Here is his central question: “What kind of human beings are we becoming?”

It is a question that deserves serious consideration in Fiji, particularly as the country seeks to position itself as a regional digital hub.

That very same concern found local expression this week in a letter published in The Fiji Times by Brother Fergus Garrett.

Writing ahead of day two of the AI conference, Brother Fergus questioned whether the programme sufficiently reflected perspectives beyond technology and business.

“The upcoming list of speakers at the AI Conference is lacking in essential input from the humanities, especially philosophy, sociology and psychology,” he wrote.

His concern was not directed against innovation itself. Rather, it was about balance.

While business values such as efficiency, productivity and innovation remain important, he argued that equal attention must be given to the social and human consequences of AI, including emerging research into its psychological, educational and societal impacts.

His observation echoes one of the encyclical’s most significant themes.

Instead, he challenges societies to ensure that technological progress does not outpace moral reflection.

In many ways, Brother Fergus’ letter serves as a timely local reminder that Fiji’s AI conversation should involve more than engineers, software developers and corporate executives.

Philosophers, educators, psychologists, sociologists, ethicists, church leaders and community organisations also have important contributions to make.

Perhaps the most striking aspect of Magnifica Humanitas is that AI itself is not presented as the central issue.

Instead, Pope Leo consistently redirects attention towards human dignity.

Rather than asking whether AI can perform certain tasks, he asks whether there are responsibilities that should never be delegated to machines.

Across the world, AI is increasingly being used to assist with recruitment, education, healthcare, policing and public administration.

While these applications promise greater efficiency, they also raise difficult questions about fairness, accountability and human judgement.

The Pope argues that people must never become secondary to algorithms.

Every person’s worth, he wrote, is intrinsic and cannot be measured solely by productivity, intelligence, wealth or technological usefulness.

That message carries particular significance for developing countries where economic pressures can sometimes encourage technological adoption without adequate consideration of long-term social consequences.

The Pacific Fiber Conference rightly highlighted the importance of building AI-ready infrastructure and expanding digital connectivity across the region.

Reliable fibre networks, improved internet access and digital innovation are essential if Pacific nations are to participate meaningfully in the global economy.

However, Pope Leo cautions against assuming that technological progress automatically produces moral progress.

History offers numerous examples where remarkable technological achievements have also generated new forms of inequality, exploitation or conflict.

The Industrial Revolution transformed economies while exposing workers to harsh conditions before labour protections emerged.

The Pope suggests AI represents a comparable turning point.

item.description: The first drops of rain had already begun to fall when we arrived at Bau Landing just after dawn. It was a little after 6am on Thursday, July 23. I had left home earlier carrying a sevusevu, waiting by the roadside for transport before making the journey east.
item.content:encoded:
The first drops of rain had already begun to fall when we arrived at Bau Landing just after dawn.

It was a little after 6am on Thursday, July 23. I had left home earlier carrying a sevusevu, waiting by the roadside for transport before making the journey east.

Beside me was photographer Timoci Dawai, affectionately known as Jim, our cameras and notebooks packed away against the damp morning.

Grey clouds hung low over the Rewa Delta as a cool wind swept across the water. It was hardly inviting weather for a boat ride, yet no one seemed discouraged.

Instead, there was a quiet sense of purpose.

Before long, we found ourselves helping women from the household of the Roko Tui Bau carry baskets, mats and ceremonial gifts aboard the boat bound for Bau Island. It was a simple act, but one that immediately reminded us that this was not merely an event to be observed. It was a communal obligation shared by everyone with a place in the vanua.

We had travelled to witness one of Fiji’s oldest surviving customary ceremonies – the duki.

For many Fijians, the word duki is familiar, yet few have had the opportunity to witness the ceremony firsthand.

Traditional herald and spokesman of the Turaga na Vunivalu na Tui Kaba, Tunitoga Aisea Jack Komaitai, explained that the duki signifies the lifting of the tabu placed on Bau’s traditional fishing grounds following the death of a high-ranking chief.

“I know that almost all members of the media were present here earlier this year during the burial of the Turaga mai Naisogolaca, former President and Speaker of Parliament, Ratu Epeli Nailatikau,” he said.

Following the burial, the liga tabu – the traditional grave diggers and custodians of chiefly funeral rites – entered the waters surrounding Bau.

Their symbolic act marked the beginning of a traditional fishing prohibition over the surrounding qoliqoli.

Only after the duki is performed can that restriction be lifted.

Mr Komaitai said this custom is reserved only for chiefs and chiefly women of the highest rank within Bau.

“The duki performed for the late Ratu Epeli comes after 100 days of mourning,” he said.

“Sometimes it can even stretch to a year, depending on discussions between the bereaved family and the vanua.”

The ceremonies that began with the duki eventually culminated in the vakataraisulu on Saturday, July 25, formally bringing to a close the traditional mourning observances for the chiefly household of Naisogolaca.

To an outsider, the duki may appear to centre on fishing.

Mr Komaitai explained that every stage of the ceremony follows customs handed down by Bau’s ancestors without alteration.

“Everything performed is according to the ancient customs passed down to us by our ancestors. Nothing new is added,” he said.

Preparation for the ceremony begins well before participants enter the water.

Those involved observe vakatatabu – traditional restrictions requiring participants to abstain from certain activities during the period leading up to the ceremony.

For women, this includes abstaining from intimacy with their husbands or partners, among other customary obligations.

Such practices, Mr Komaitai said, reinforce discipline, respect and spiritual readiness before undertaking an important duty for the vanua.

The ceremony is therefore as much about personal commitment as it is about communal participation.

Perhaps the strongest message emerging from Bau was that the success of the duki depends not on individuals, but on collective unity.

Everyone from Bau’s three villages participated.

That included those born on the island, members of the chiefly household and those who had married into the community.

“The important factor is that all those participating need to be united and bonded closely in regard to the ceremony and their duty to the vanua,” Mr Komaitai said.

He also drew parallels with Christian teachings.
